walkthroughs.title: Two long bears
steps: March 10, 2000. The Nasdaq closes at 5,048.62. It doesn't bottom until October 9, 2002, at 1,114.11.
Next time it's the S&P 500. It falls 57% from its October 2007 peak to its March 2009 trough.
Neither was one fast drop. Both ground on for more than a year, and that's what wears you out.

walkthroughs.title: Rallies inside a bear
steps: Bears bounce, and the bounces are fast and sharp. That's what pulls people back in.
In 2001 the Nasdaq ran almost 40% between April and the end of May. By September it was at new lows.
From mid-2000 on, every big rally topped under the last one. Lower highs and lower lows: that's a downtrend.

walkthroughs.title: How a bear ends
steps: A downtrend holds until price makes a higher low, then takes out the last rally high.
After the October 2002 low, the Nasdaq held a higher low in March. In early May it cleared its November high.
You only see the bottom in hindsight. Waiting for that gets you in late, but on evidence, not a guess.
Even then it's a possible turn, not a sure one.

questions.q: Marking up the Nasdaq in 2001, what do you need to see before you call it a downtrend?
choices: One straight drop to the low
questions.why: Lower highs and lower lows. You need both. Every rally tops out under the last one, and every drop breaks the last low. Lower highs with rising lows is just the range getting tighter. And don't expect a straight line. Rallies inside a bear are fast and sharp, and they're what fool people. Here's how I read it. Mark each rally top and each low. When each top prints under the last and each low breaks the last, it's a downtrend, whatever the headlines say.
questions.lesson_line: Mark the tops and the lows. Lower and lower is a downtrend, bounces and all.

wrong.Higher highs and higher lows: That's the opposite. Higher highs and higher lows is an uptrend, the kind of chart we want to be buying.
wrong.Lower highs and higher lows: The lows are rising there. That's the range tightening, not a downtrend. You need the lower lows too.
wrong.One straight drop to the low: Bears don't fall in a straight line. They bounce, often hard, and the bounces are what trap people.

A big rally inside a downtrend proves nothing until it holds a higher low and clears the last rally high.

It's to still have your money when the next bull starts.

questions.q: Everyone remembers 2008 as the crash year. When did the Great Recession itself start and end?
questions.why: December 2007 to June 2009. Those are the NBER's dates, the group that officially dates US recessions. Now put the market next to it. The S&P 500 topped in October 2007, before the recession started. It bottomed in March 2009, three months before the recession ended. Stocks look ahead. Wait for the economy to tell you it's bad, and price already told you months earlier. Same on the way up. I watch the index, not the headlines.
questions.lesson_line: Stocks turn before the economy does. Watch price, not the recession calendar.

questions.q: The Nasdaq's top close came in March 2000 and its low close in October 2002. How long did that bear grind on?
questions.why: About 31 months. Count it: 2000 to 2002 is 2 years, so 24 months, and March to October adds 7 more. The top close was 5,048.62 on March 10, 2000. The low close was 1,114.11 on October 9, 2002. More than a year in, it was still making new lows, 1,638.80 on April 4, 2001. That's the part people underestimate.
